analysis.body:
# Grid Interconnection Queue Snapshot for AI Infrastructure Analysis

Across five major US grid operators, 8,372 generation and storage projects totaling 1.33 million megawatts await interconnection as of September 10, 2026. This queue—comprising everything from solar farms to gas plants to battery systems—represents planned supply seeking to meet future demand. While the queue is not a direct measure of data center electricity consumption, the composition signals infrastructure trends relevant to large load centers: storage projects total 328,106 MW across all operators, and natural gas accounts for 184,544 MW. Texas leads by absolute capacity with 438,086 MW in queue (78,092 MW of which is gas), followed by New York at 319,095 MW and MISO's footprint at 299,721 MW. Commercial-sector electricity sales in June 2026 reached 54,797 MWh across eight states, with California consuming the most at 10,024 MWh but Texas paying the lowest average price at $8.66 per megawatt-hour.

The regional variation in gas and storage buildout hints at infrastructure positioning around demand clusters. ERCOT's queue is 17.8 percent gas and 36.5 percent storage and renewable; MISO's is 10 percent gas and 40 percent storage and renewable. SPP shows 23.9 percent gas versus 59 percent wind and storage combined. CAISO, serving the highest-priced market at $27.33 per MWh in California, has only 1.3 percent gas in queue but 65.5 percent storage, reflecting both constrained transmission and state-level clean energy requirements. NYISO's queue is heavily weighted toward "other" projects (291,136 MW), a category the source does not disaggregate, making that region's buildout profile opaque.

Pricing spreads correlate loosely with queue composition: the lowest-cost states (Texas at $8.66, Oregon at $10.59) sit in regions building proportionally more gas; the highest-cost state (California at $27.33) is forced into storage and imports. These interconnection queues typically process over multi-year timescales, meaning projects stamped today may not energize for three to five years. Track monthly updates to gas allocations in ERCOT and SPP queues, and watch whether CAISO's "other" category disaggregates, as both signal whether grid operators expect sustained demand growth aligned with data center build cycles.
